items.statement:
Assume full AC. Let $F_0,F_1\subset S^3$ be compact smooth embedded spanning surfaces for the same nonempty link $L$, with supplied radial collars in disjoint smooth normal tubes of $L$. Orient each component of $L$ arbitrarily, orient the tube boundary tori by their outward normal toward the link exterior, and orient the two surface boundary curves compatibly with $L$. Let $\alpha$ be a smooth proper transverse common arc in the exterior, transverse to its boundary, with transverse boundary-curve crossings at its distinct endpoints. Extend it radially to an isolated smooth embedded arc $A$ ending on $L$. Suppose its two ordered endpoint intersection signs agree, so their sum is $2$ or $-2$.

For every open neighborhood $U$ of $A$ there are a smooth closed ball $B\subset U$ with $A\subset\operatorname{int}B$ and a continuous surjection $q:S^3\to S^3$, fixed off $\operatorname{int}B$, such that its only non-singleton fiber is $A$, $q(B)=B$, and
$$(B,q((F_0\cup F_1)\cap B))\cong(B^3,B^3\cap\{z=0\}).$$
Thus this actual local surface image is a properly embedded locally flat disk, including at the collapsed point. The surfaces may be disconnected or nonorientable. No definiteness or primeness assumption is needed for this local assertion.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. For each $p\in M$, let
$\gamma_p:I_p\to M$ be the maximal integral curve through $p$, and set

$$ \mathcal D:=\{(t,p)\in\mathbb R\times M:t\in I_p\}, \qquad \Phi(t,p):=\gamma_p(t). $$

Then $\mathcal D$ is open in $\mathbb R\times M$, each fibre $\mathcal D_p$ is
an interval containing $0$, the map $\Phi:\mathcal D\to M$ is smooth, and
$\Phi$ is the unique maximal local flow generated by $X$.

Assume countable choice. Let $L\subset S^3$ be a smooth link with chosen disjoint smooth normal tubes, and let $F_0,F_1$ be smooth embedded spanning surfaces with boundary $L$. Orient each component of $L$ arbitrarily. Supply radial collar coordinates in the tubes in which each surface collar is given by a smooth ray direction depending on the boundary parameter. Put $X=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu L$, and orient each torus of $\partial\nu L$ as the boundary of the oriented solid tube, so its outward normal points into $X$. Orient the two surface boundary curves on those tori compatibly with $L$.

Let $\alpha$ be a smoothly and properly embedded arc of transverse intersection of $F_0\cap X$ and $F_1\cap X$, transverse to $\partial X$, with transverse boundary-curve crossings at its distinct endpoints. Extend it radially through the supplied collars to the corresponding points of $L$, obtaining a smooth embedded arc $A$. Assume a neighborhood of this extended arc contains no other intersection components. Write $i_0,i_1\in\{1,-1\}$ for the ordered local intersection signs of the two boundary curves at its endpoints, measured on $\partial\nu L$.

The union $F_0\cup F_1$ has a closed intrinsic neighborhood $K$ of $A$ modeled by four pages with common arc, glued at each end by one of the matchings $M=(01)(23)$ and $N=(03)(12)$, with pages zero and two on $F_0$ and pages one and three on $F_1$. The two end matchings differ if and only if $i_0=i_1$. Consequently collapsing $A$ in this neighborhood gives a closed topological disk exactly when $i_0+i_1=2$ or $-2$. When $i_0+i_1=0$ it gives two disks joined at their interior centers. For the standard cases the ambient arc-collapse map can be chosen supported in any prescribed neighborhood of $A$, and its image of $K$ is an embedded topological disk. Local flatness of that disk is not asserted here.

Let $\alpha:[-1,1]\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth embedding with nonvanishing derivative, smooth in boundary charts at both endpoints, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of its image $A$. Then there is a continuous surjection $q:S^3\to S^3$, fixed on $S^3\setminus U$, whose only non-singleton fiber is $A$. In particular the quotient space $S^3/A$, obtained by identifying exactly the points of $A$ to one point, is homeomorphic to $S^3$.

Moreover there is a continuous family $Q:S^3\times[0,1]\to S^3$ with $Q_0=\operatorname{id}$ and $Q_1=q$, fixed on $S^3\setminus U$, such that every $Q_t$ for $0\le t<1$ is a homeomorphism. Every closed parameter interval $[0,t_0]$ with $t_0<1$ therefore gives an ambient topological isotopy. The assertion concerns a topological quotient; it does not assert that the terminal map is a diffeomorphism or that an arbitrary surface containing the arc becomes a surface after collapse.

Assume full AC. Fix a finite cyclic subdivision of $S^1$ into edges. Let $c:S^1\times(0,1]\to S^2$ be continuous, with each $c_r$ an embedding. On every closed edge require that $c$ extends smoothly to an open neighborhood of that edge times each compact positive-radius interval, and has nonzero edge tangent there. At each subdivision vertex require the two one-sided tangent lines of $c_r$ to be distinct for every $r>0$; the family is smooth away from these finitely many corners. Then
$$D=\{0\}\cup\{r c_r(s):s\in S^1,\ 0<r\le1\}$$
forms a standard ball-disk pair: there is a homeomorphism $(B^3,D)\cong(B^3,B^3\cap\{z=0\})$. In particular it is a properly embedded locally flat closed topological disk. There need be no positive lower bound on corner angles as $r\downarrow0$.

More precisely a radius-preserving homeomorphism of $B^3$ carries $D$ to a disk supplied by a smooth positive-radius family of embedded circles. If the subdivision has no corners and the family is already smooth, this preliminary homeomorphism may be the identity.

derivations.claim: Choose a proper strip around $A$ on $F_0$. Explicitly take a smooth transverse field along that interval, tangent to $L$ at its ends, extend it in finitely many surface charts tangent to the boundary, and use its short flow in [F1]. Normalize its restriction at each end to the unit boundary tangent, with whichever sign is continuous along the strip. Its flow coordinates give $c_0(x,y)$, $-1\le x\le1$, $|y|<\delta$, with $c_0(x,0)=A(x)$ and with the two end edges on $L$. Extend this map slightly across its end faces in the original smooth boundary charts, patching extensions off the prescribed strip if necessary. The strip is orientable, so its two tangent vectors define a smooth unit ambient normal. Its short normal exponential map gives a smooth ambient chart $(x,y,z)$ by [F1] and compact injectivity, with $F_0$ given by $z=0$, $-1\le x\le1$, and the two short pieces of $L$ by $x=\pm1,z=0$. The chart can be taken inside $U$, missing every other sheet of either embedded surface; locally these are the given surface charts, and compactness of the arc supplies a common sufficiently small width.

On $F_1$ near $A$, the ambient coordinate $x$ is a submersion, since its derivative on $\dot A$ is one. Choose a nonzero smooth field in its one-dimensional kernel along $A$, and extend it nearby while retaining $dx=0$. One obtains this by subtracting the $x$ component with a local field having $dx=1$, then patching the kernel fields in finitely many charts, close enough to their fixed nonzero values along $A$. At the two end edges the kernel is exactly tangent to $L$, so choose its boundary value to be $\sigma_\pm\partial_y$, $\sigma_\pm\in\{1,-1\}$, with the sign continuous from the interior. Its flow from [F1] gives an actual parametrization $c_1(x,t)=(x,Y(x,t),Z(x,t))$, with $(Y,Z)(x,0)=0$ and with $Y(\pm1,t)=\sigma_\pm t$, $Z(\pm1,t)=0$. The two transverse derivatives $(Y_t,Z_t)$ are never simultaneously zero along the compact arc. The formula $v(x,t)=\int_0^1(Y_t,Z_t)(x,ut)\,du$ gives $(Y,Z)=t\,v(x,t)$ with smooth $v$ and $|v|>0$ on a uniform smaller strip. Thus its normal radius is $R(x,t)=|t|a(x,t)$ for smooth $a=|v|>0$, and shrinking makes $a+t a_t>0$ uniformly. It is strictly increasing on each positive transverse half and strictly decreasing on each negative half.

Take the closed confocal ellipsoids $E_\rho=\{x^2/(1+\rho^2)+(y^2+z^2)/\rho^2\le1\}$ for $0<\rho\le\varepsilon$, choosing $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small with strict margins inside the chart and the two strips. On either surface a point of $\partial E_\rho$ with axial coordinate $x\in[-1,1]$ has normal radius $R_\rho(x)=\rho\sqrt{1-x^2/(1+\rho^2)}>0$. By step 2.1, for each $x$ there is exactly one point of each transverse half of $F_1$ at this radius. For $F_0$ the two points are simply $y=\pm R_\rho(x),z=0$. Existence is uniform because $R_\rho\le\rho$ and the radii at the two fixed outer strip edges have a positive common lower bound. The implicit inverse in [F1] shows that these four edges, parametrized by $x\in[-1,1]$, depend smoothly on $x,\rho$ for $\rho>0$, including their endpoints; each is regular since its first coordinate is $x$. There are no surface points with $x$ beyond these end faces in this neighborhood: both surfaces have boundary exactly on those faces and point inward along $A$.

At $x=\pm1$ the radius is $\rho^2/\sqrt{1+\rho^2}$. Hence the four edge ends lie at the two points $y=\pm\rho^2/\sqrt{1+\rho^2},z=0$ on each end piece of $L$, with the same page pairings as in [F2]. Distinct pairings make their union $C_\rho$ one embedded circle. Its four corners have distinct tangent lines. Indeed boundary-curve transversality at the original arc endpoints says that the difference of the two radial angle functions has nonzero derivative there. For sufficiently small nonzero displacement along $L$, their angle difference is nonzero modulo $\pi$, so the two surface tangent planes at each of these corner points are distinct, meeting exactly in $TL$. Also $L$ is transverse to $\partial E_\rho$: its coordinate tangent is $\partial_y$ and the derivative of the ellipsoid equation in that direction is $2y/\rho^2\ne0$. If the two edge tangent lines on the ellipsoid agreed, that common line would lie in $TL\cap T\partial E_\rho=0$, a contradiction. This proves the required corner independence for every $0<\rho\le\varepsilon$ after shrinking once. The strict margins also permit a short extension past the outer radius.

Use the actual confocal-ellipsoid collapse of [F3] in this adapted chart. It fixes $\partial E_\varepsilon$ and the outside, collapses exactly $A$, and sends $E_\rho$ to $(\rho/\varepsilon)E_\varepsilon$. On each positive level its restriction is the invertible linear map $(x,y,z)\mapsto(\rho\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}\,x/(\varepsilon\sqrt{1+\rho^2}),y,z)$. Therefore it carries the four edges of $C_\rho$ to a regular four-edge circle with the same distinct corner tangent lines and smooth dependence on every positive $\rho$. Apply the fixed diagonal linear rescaling $E_\varepsilon\to B^3$ and put $r=\rho/\varepsilon$. These image circles are now exactly a finite-corner radial family satisfying [F4]; their cyclic edge ordering is fixed by the two end matchings and does not change with radius.

Let $K=(F_0\cup F_1)\cap E_\varepsilon$. The level description in step 3.1 shows that it consists exactly of $A$ and the circles $C_\rho$, $0<\rho\le\varepsilon$. Thus after the collapse and diagonal rescaling its entire image, not just selected levels, is the radial disk in [F4]. That supplier gives a homeomorphism of the ball-disk pair to the standard pair. Pull back the diagonal rescaling to conclude that $(E_\varepsilon,q(K))$ is a standard ball-disk pair. Set $B$ to be this ellipsoid in the original ambient chart and extend the collapse by the identity outside it, as in [F3]. It is supported in $U$, has just $A$ as a nonsingleton fiber, and maps $B$ to itself. This proves the local flatness and all asserted support and fiber properties. Every construction used only the two local strips, so neither connectedness nor orientability of the complete surfaces was required.

boundaries.reason: An actual isolated smooth common arc with two endpoints is supplied.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 5.1–6.1 collapse exactly A at radius zero and apply the actual radial-family criterion to all positive levels.
Step 4.1 uses distinct end matchings to make the four level edges one circle.

boundaries.reason: Proper transverse exterior intersection, transverse boundary crossings, smooth radial extension and equal endpoint signs are explicit hypotheses.

boundaries.evidence: Step 4.1 computes actual end-corner coordinates and independent tangents from 2y/rho²≠0.
Steps 1.1–2.1 use compact smooth flows; step 6.1 inherits full AC through the cornered radial-family supplier.

axioms.use: Full AC is inherited from the finite-corner radial-circle criterion and its plane Jordan–Schönflies supplier. It supplies countable choice for compact smooth flows. The actual chart, level curves and arc-collapse formula use finite constructions.

risk_review.notes: Actual F0-adapted chart, F1 flow in ker dx, uniform monotone normal radius, explicit confocal levels and corner independence supplied. Uses the reviewed arc helper constructive formula in any supplied chart; not just existence of arbitrary quotient.

constructive_supplier_evidence.exact_read_body:
1.1 Extend the embedding a little past each endpoint inside a smooth endpoint chart; shrink the two added intervals until the extended arc remains embedded and lies in $U$. Compactness separates the two new ends from the original arc outside their endpoint charts, so this is possible. Along the extended interval choose a smooth oriented orthonormal frame $e_1(s),e_2(s)$ perpendicular to the arc tangent inside $TS^3$. This requires only finite constructions: project two appropriate constant coordinate vectors to the normal planes on each small interval, apply Gram–Schmidt there, choose a finite ordered interval subdivision subordinate to these charts, and glue consecutive frames. On an overlap their transition is a smooth plane rotation; its angle has a smooth real lift on a sufficiently short overlapping interval. Rotate the new frame through that lifted angle using a smooth cutoff, agreeing with the old one near the gluing point. Finitely many such interpolations produce the frame on the whole interval. No endpoint frame has been prescribed, so no cyclic compatibility is required. [given, construct]

2.1 For $r=(u^2+v^2)^{1/2}$ the round normal map is $\Psi(s,u,v)=\cos r\,\alpha(s)+(\sin r/r)(u e_1(s)+v e_2(s))$, with its smooth value at $r=0$. Its derivative along the zero section has independent columns $\alpha'(s),e_1(s),e_2(s)$, so [F1] makes it a local diffeomorphism there. It is injective on some uniform short normal tube about a slightly shorter compact extended interval: otherwise collisions at radii tending to zero would, by compactness, limit to two equal arc points; their parameters agree by injectivity of the arc, and a common local inverse then excludes those collisions. Shrink the tube to lie in $U$. Thus in one smooth product chart the original arc is the straight segment $\{(x,0,0):-1\le x\le1\}$. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ so small that the closed ellipsoid $E=\{x^2/(1+\varepsilon^2)+(y^2+z^2)/\varepsilon^2\le1\}$ lies in this chart. Its slight extension beyond the segment fits inside the extended parameter interval. [step 1.1, F1, construct]

3.1 For $p=(x,y,z)\in E$ write $r^2=y^2+z^2$ and define $w(p)=(x^2+r^2-1+\sqrt{(1-x^2-r^2)^2+4r^2})/2$. This is continuous, nonnegative, zero exactly on the segment, and at most $\varepsilon^2$ on $E$. For $w>0$ it is the unique positive solution of $x^2/(1+w)+r^2/w=1$: multiplying by $w(1+w)$ gives $w^2+(1-x^2-r^2)w-r^2=0$, whose nonnegative root is the displayed value. The equation's left side is strictly decreasing in $w$ until it reaches one; at $w=\varepsilon^2$ it is at most one on $E$. On the axis outside the segment the root is $x^2-1$, while on the segment it is zero. The level $w=\rho^2>0$ is consequently the ellipsoid $p=(\sqrt{1+\rho^2}\,u_1,\rho u_2,\rho u_3)$, $u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2=1$. In particular $w=\varepsilon^2$ is exactly $\partial E$. [step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 For $0\le t\le1$ put $a_t=1-t$ and $b_t^2=(1+\varepsilon^2-a_t^2)/\varepsilon^2>0$. On $E$ define $q_t(x,y,z)=(\sqrt{(a_t^2+b_t^2w(p))/(1+w(p))}\,x,y,z)$. The formula is jointly continuous, including on the segment, where its value is $(a_t x,0,0)$. At $t=0$ it is the identity. On $\partial E$, $w=\varepsilon^2$ and $a_t^2+b_t^2\varepsilon^2=1+\varepsilon^2$, so it fixes the boundary pointwise for every $t$. Off the segment, the level parametrization in step 3.1 shows that its image is $(\sqrt{a_t^2+b_t^2\rho^2}\,u_1,\rho u_2,\rho u_3)$. [step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 If $t<1$, these image ellipsoids are strictly nested for $0<\rho\le\varepsilon$, and fill $E$ minus the shorter segment $[-a_t,a_t]\times\{0,0\}$. To verify uniqueness directly, for a point $(X,Y,Z)$ off that shorter segment solve $X^2/(a_t^2+b_t^2\rho^2)+(Y^2+Z^2)/\rho^2=1$. The left side strictly decreases from a value greater than one to a value at most one at $\rho=\varepsilon$; on the axis with $|X|>a_t$ the same assertion follows directly from the first term. Thus exactly one $\rho$ exists, and the displayed image ellipsoid determines exactly one unit vector $u$. On the shorter segment the map is the bijection $x\mapsto a_t x$ of the original segment. Hence $q_t:E\to E$ is a continuous bijection and is a homeomorphism, because $E$ is compact and Hausdorff. At $t=1$, the image ellipsoids are instead the homothetic copies $(\rho/\varepsilon)\partial E$; they fill $E\setminus\{0\}$ uniquely. The entire original segment and only it maps to zero. Thus $q_1$ is onto and has exactly the asserted fibers. [step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Transport $q_t$ through the chart in step 2.1 and extend it by the identity outside the image of $E$. The boundary equality in step 4.1 makes the resulting family $Q$ continuous on $S^3\times[0,1]$. Each slice with $t<1$ is a homeomorphism by step 5.1 and the identity gluing; its support lies in $U$. On any compact time interval avoiding one, the inverse is jointly continuous: the map $(p,t)\mapsto(Q_t(p),t)$ is a continuous bijection of the compact Hausdorff space $S^3\times[0,t_0]$ to itself, hence a homeomorphism. The terminal map $q=Q_1$ has only $A$ as a non-singleton fiber by step 5.1. It factors to a continuous bijection $S^3/A\to S^3$ by the definition of the quotient topology. That quotient is compact, and a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is closed, hence a homeomorphism. This proves the quotient and approximation assertions using the explicit formulas; a surface link at the collapsed point would require separate hypotheses. [step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct] ∎
